theme: God’s indictment; Zion’s daughters, covenant lawsuit
readingInstruction: Read Isaiah 1:1-3:26. Isaiah is the longest and most quoted prophet in the New Testament. Read the opening chapters as a courtroom scene, and listen for God’s offer in 1:18.
settingTheScene: Isaiah son of Amoz prophesied in Jerusalem during the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, roughly 740 to 690 BC. He was probably a man of standing in the city, with access to kings. The book that bears his name has sixty-six chapters, and it falls into two great halves: judgment and the Assyrian crisis in chapters 1 to 39, and comfort and the coming Servant in chapters 40 to 66. The first chapter works as a summary of the whole.
observation: “Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth; for the LORD has spoken: Children have I reared and brought up, but they have rebelled against me” (1:2).
“The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s crib, but Israel does not know, my people do not understand” (1:3).
“Bring no more vain offerings; incense is an abomination to me” (1:13).
“Learn to do good; seek justice, correct oppression; bring justice to the fatherless, plead the widow’s cause” (1:17).
“Come now, let us reason together, says the LORD: though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow” (1:18).
“How the faithful city has become a whore” (1:21).
“He shall judge between the nations, and shall decide disputes for many peoples; and they shall beat their swords into plowshares” (2:4).
“Stop regarding man in whose nostrils is breath, for of what account is he?” (2:22).
interpretation:
The prophet opens with God calling heaven and earth as witnesses, as in Deuteronomy. The charge is rebellion by children who have been loved and raised. The comparison is humbling: an ox and a donkey know where their food comes from, but Israel does not. The nation is sick from head to foot, with wounds that no one has treated. They are like Sodom, spared only because a few survived.

The religion of the people is another problem. They keep the feasts, offer the sacrifices, spread out their hands in prayer. And God says he cannot stand it. This does not mean God rejects worship. It means worship from people who plot evil and ignore the oppressed is an offense. Hosea 6:6 and Micah 6:8, which you just read, say the same. The remedy is practical: learn to do good, seek justice, correct oppression, defend the fatherless, plead for the widow.

Then comes one of the great invitations in the Bible. “Come now, let us reason together.” God does not simply condemn. He argues, he offers, and he promises. “Though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow.” The cleansing that no sacrifice by itself could provide is offered freely, on the condition that they are willing and obedient. The choice is plain: eat the good of the land, or be devoured by the sword.

Chapter 2 sets a vision of the last days beside the failure of the present. The nations will stream to the mountain of the LORD, as in Micah 4. Then the prophet turns to the pride of Judah: idols, wealth, horses, and haughty looks. God will humble all that is lofty. The day of the LORD is against everything proud. Chapter 3 describes the collapse of social order, with children as leaders and women of Zion strutting in finery that will be replaced by sackcloth.
connection: Jesus quoted Isaiah’s description of hollow worship: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Mark 7:6, from Isaiah 29:13). Revelation 7:14 speaks of those whose robes have been washed in the blood of the Lamb and made white. 1 John 1:7-9 promises that the blood of Jesus cleanses us from all sin. James 1:27 defines pure religion as visiting orphans and widows in their affliction.
application:
Memorize Isaiah 1:18 and take it as a personal invitation. Name a sin that you carry, and bring it to God.

Choose one act of justice or mercy this week: help a widow, a child, or someone who is being treated unfairly.

Examine your worship. Is there any area where your religious activity is not matched by how you live?
prayerPrompts: Confess where you have rebelled as one of God’s children.
Ask him to reason with you and wash your sins white.
Thank him for his invitation to come.
